newsitem.title: FRANCE: Questions still hang over French economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Questions still hang over French economic policy.

text.p: The exclusion of Communists from key posts in the French cabinet was reassuring for financial markets but big concerns remain about the new leftwing government's economic programme, economists said on Wednesday.

The rainbow pink-red-green lineup formed by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin after the broad left coalition ousted President Jacques Chirac's right-wing allies in Sunday's parliamentary election contained few surprises, economists said.

"The cabinet is perfectly in line" with what was expected, said economist Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "We have to hope once they have been in power some time they will prove to be less dangerous than they could potentially be."

The markets' worries focus on how far the government will go toward transforming its electoral platform stressing jobs and economic growth -- aimed at tackling record 12.8 percent unemployment -- into policy.

Bonds and stocks showed scant reaction in after-hours trade to the appointment of Socialists, Greens and Communists to the cabinet made up of 14 ministers, two ministers-delegate and 10 secretaries of state. The French franc weakened a tenth of a centime against the German currency to 3.330 per mark.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, architect of the Socialists' economic policy which pledged to create 700,000 youth jobs and chop the work week to 35 hours from 39 without cutting pay, was given the important portfolio of finance and industry.

He has advocated flexibility in meeting Maastricht treaty conditions on monetary union calling for public deficits to be cut to three percent of gross domestic product. He has also urged a slightly "softer" euro to boost job creation.
Strauss-Kahn's appointment means "we can already start to forget the budget criterion" in the Maastricht treaty, Hugues de Montvalon, economist at brokers Oddo et Cie, said.
The new finance minister was regarded by markets as a safe, experienced pair of hands, although "not as a free marketeer in the U.S. or UK sense," said Steven Englander of Smith Barney.
Socialist Martine Aubry got the number two cabinet berth and will head a superministry for employment and social security.
Communist Jean-Claude Gayssot, best known for co-authoring a tough anti-racism law, became transport minister while party comrade Marie-George Buffet was named sports and youth minister.

Jospin needed the Communists to clinch a majority in the 577-member parliament. It was the first time Communists have been in the cabinet since 1984 but they have ministries carrying little clout to pursue their opposition to monetary union.
"The nomination of Communist ministers to relatively minor posts will make very little difference," said Owens-Thomsen.

"But there are definitely risks in this government," she said. "You have those elements in the government which are anti-Maastricht, in favour of increased spending. Obviously these are things to worry about," she said.

Dominique Voynet, the iron lady of the Greens, was named environment minister while Emile Zuccarelli of the centre-left Radical Socialist Party, was appointed minister of the civil service, administrative reform and decentralisation.
Jean-Pierre Chevenement, leader of the Citizens' Movement which opposes the single currency, was named interior minister.

While supporting monetary union, Jospin is against more austerity to fulfill the strict deficit conditions to qualify. He also wants to renegotiate the "stability pact" meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of a single currency. That agreement is due to be ratified in Amsterdam in mid-June.
Other market worries include campaign pledges to halt privatisation, boost consumers' purchasing power and increase controls on the ability of firms to lay off workers.
